analysis.one_liner: Strips presidential power to protect offshore waters from oil and gas drilling and voids past protections.
analysis.headline: The bill has not advanced past a House subcommittee hearing; it would strip past presidential protections on offshore lands and cap future ones.
analysis.plain_summary: Presidents have long used their authority under the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act to take stretches of federal ocean water off the table for oil and gas drilling. This bill would erase several of those protections — covering Arctic, Atlantic, Pacific, and Bering Sea areas, including withdrawals signed as recently as January 6, 2025 — and would tightly limit any future president's ability to make similar protections. It caps protected areas at 150,000 acres at a time, requires Congress's approval for anything larger, lets Congress quickly overturn any withdrawal, and requires detailed Interior Department studies before a withdrawal.
analysis.who_benefits: Offshore oil and gas companies gain the most: protected federal waters in the Arctic, Atlantic, Gulf of Mexico, and Bering Sea become available for leasing, and future administrations cannot easily take new areas off the table. Gulf Coast leaseholders and state revenue recipients also gain from expanded lease sales.

how_it_helps.text: It immediately nullifies eight Obama- and Biden-era presidential memoranda and executive orders that withdrew Arctic, Atlantic, Pacific, and Bering Sea areas from oil and gas leasing, re-opening those waters to leasing without a new lease sale process.

Going forward, it caps presidential withdrawals at 150,000 acres each, 500,000 acres cumulatively without Congress, and 20 years in duration, and requires extensive Interior Department assessments before any withdrawal.
It gives Congress a fast-track procedure to overturn any presidential withdrawal by joint resolution, and bars the President from withdrawing areas already scheduled for lease sales.

analysis.who_pays: Coastal communities, fishing interests, and tourism economies in areas opened to drilling bear the spill and industrialization risk; the public loses a long-standing, if executive-branch, tool for protecting federal waters, including areas of cultural importance in the Bering Sea.

drawbacks.text: The bill permanently narrows a protection tool every president has used, capping withdrawals at 150,000 acres at a time (vs. protections covering millions of acres) and barring any withdrawal longer than 20 years, which would leave long-lived protections effectively unavailable.

It would nullify existing withdrawals covering Arctic, Atlantic, and Bering Sea waters, opening areas that earlier administrations set aside for climate, fishery, and coastal-protection reasons to oil and gas leasing, with spillover risks for fishing, coastal tourism, and marine ecosystems.

The bill strips judicial review of withdrawal decisions under its disapproval procedures and rigs Senate floor procedures for disapproval resolutions, which opponents would view as entrenching development decisions beyond ordinary checks.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefit, in its sponsors' terms, is more domestic energy production and federal revenue. The costs are the loss of presidential and congressional power to protect specific waters from drilling, the opening of protected Arctic, Atlantic, and Pacific areas that earlier administrations—both parties—had set aside, and the exposure of coastal communities and fisheries to spill and industrialization risks. It is also a large, permanent shift of constitutional authority over public waters from the President toward whichever Congress holds power, which would bind future majorities of both parties.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to two House committees in January 2025; four months later it went to the Energy and Mineral Resources Subcommittee, which held a hearing in May 2025, and nothing further has happened.

narrative.text: H.R. 513 was introduced on January 16, 2025 by Rep. Clay Higgins with 25 Republican cosponsors.
It was referred to the House Natural Resources and Rules Committees, and on May 13, 2025 was referred to the Energy and Mineral Resources Subcommittee.
On May 20, 2025, the subcommittee held a hearing on the bill; no markup, committee vote, or floor action has occurred since.

The bill would nullify eight presidential memoranda and executive orders withdrawing Arctic, Atlantic, and Bering Sea areas from oil and gas leasing, including orders signed in December 2016, December 2014, March 2023, and January 6, 2025.

It would amend the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act to cap presidential withdrawals at 150,000 acres at a time and 500,000 acres cumulatively without congressional approval, limit them to 20 years, require Interior Department assessments first, and let Congress overturn any withdrawal by joint resolution.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one's situation has changed; if it becomes law, offshore oil and gas producers gain access to protected waters, while coastal and Alaska Native communities lose protections they relied on.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Nobody yet; oil drillers would if it passes

for.name: House Natural Resources Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources
for.what_they_did: Held a hearing on the bill on May 20, 2025, the only action since referral.

sides.party_line_note: All 26 sponsors and cosponsors are Republicans, and no Democrat has signed on; no votes have occurred yet, so the partisan shape is so far one-sided.

industries.note: The bill nullifies withdrawals that kept parts of the Arctic, Atlantic, Gulf, and Pacific shelves off-limits and makes it much harder for future presidents to protect new areas, enlarging the acreage available to lease and drill. Its sponsor represents a Gulf Coast oil and gas state.

industries.industry: Commercial fishing and Bering Sea coastal communities
industries.note: Nullifying the Northern Bering Sea climate resilience order (EO 13754) opens waters that Alaska Native and fishing communities fought to shield from industrial activity, risking disruption to fisheries and subsistence resources.
Expanded leasing in Atlantic, Pacific, and Gulf waters increases the long-term risk of spills and drilling infrastructure near shorelines that tourism and recreation economies depend on.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has only reached a subcommittee hearing in a chamber where Republicans hold a narrow majority; major amendments to the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act rarely become law on their own, though parts could travel on a broader energy bill. With no Democratic cosponsors, its prospects for becoming law in this form are uncertain.
